This Investing Strategy Is So Good You Can’t Handle It
 
Plus, it’s bank earnings-palooza
 

Wall Street has found a way to take our minds off sagging chip stocks, scarce diesel and midterm elections—its own earnings. The biggest U.S. banks and asset managers will unveil their quarterly results over the next few days. How they and their clients handled a volatile period will make for interesting reading. You can follow along here. Stock futures are mixed, with tech echoing Monday’s weakness but other pockets of the market resilient.

Like eating a habanero

 

Mae West said that “too much of a good thing can be wonderful.”

 

Well, maybe. A case in point is taking a good stock investment strategy and combining it with another good one and then another. Instead of canceling each other out, Wes Crill, a senior investment executive at Dimensional Fund Advisors, found that three well-known drivers of extra returns more or less stacked up, producing a truly wonderful outcome.

 

The factors are small stocks, low relative price and high profitability. Combining them resulted in an annualized return of 17.1% since July 1963.

 

That compares with 10.9% for U.S. stocks generally. Through this July, Crill’s hypothetical combo would have grown a $10,000 investment into $208 million before taxes and fees, or more than 30 times as much as U.S. stocks overall. 

 

But Crill invokes a different Hollywood icon—Jack Nicholson in “A Few Good Men”—to explain why nobody would have stuck it out.

 

“You can’t handle the tracking error!”

 

Since there aren’t too many stocks that tick all three boxes, the small number turned out to be frighteningly volatile relative to the market—no picnic itself sometimes. To earn an extra 6.3 percentage points annually, the portfolio trailed by as much as 38.4 points over a 12-month period and by a gut-wrenching 72.6 points over 36 months.

 

In theory, a young investor could lock away their paychecks in such a strategy until retirement day and never open an account statement. They’d have to be confident, though, that they’d never need to tap their savings in an emergency. 

 

The future won’t look like the past, of course, and Crill didn’t highlight these results to sell a new product anyway.

 

Instead, it’s a useful way to respond to clients who ask him why lots of smart investors haven’t snatched away all of the excess-return hacks that finance professors have identified. It’s uncomfortable.

 

“That’s my best explanation for why this persists,” says Crill.

 

Just buying and holding a plain vanilla index fund is hard too. And good returns aren’t guaranteed, either. An investor with truly unlucky timing could have sat tight for decades and earned less than ultrasafe bonds.

 

That possibility underscores why sprinkling in Crill’s winning factors could be useful. Every little bit of extra return makes stock investing easier to stomach.

 

The analogy Crill uses is having a habanero pepper in your kitchen. Eating one is too much, but adding a small bit to a dish can spice up a portfolio without causing intestinal distress.
